Market liquidity appears to be declining.

The G10 Excess Liquidity Leading Indicator has turned negative for the first time since 2024.

This metric compares the rate of money supply growth across G10 economies with the pace of economic growth.

When the money supply grows faster than the economy, there is excess liquidity that can support asset prices.

Historically, this gauge has led the performance of the semiconductor index, $SOX, by roughly 6 months.

If this historical relationship holds, it points to weaker semiconductor stock performance over the coming months.

Keep watching liquidity.

El Niño just got declared, and forecasters are calling this one a Super El Niño.

This is a food-price story before it is a weather story. Droughts and floods wreck harvests, so the smart money skips the coffee and wheat futures and buys the companies that sell farmers the tools to grow through bad soil.

Croda International (CRDA LN) makes the crop-protection and seed-enhancement chemicals that keep crops alive in saltier, drier ground. The market has left it for dead, down more than half from its 2023 peak, and it pays about 3.3% while you wait.

The bigger picture: El Niño on food, plus the Strait of Hormuz on oil, is a 1970s-style inflation pulse landing on a slowing economy. That is stagflation, and the last time it hit, materials, energy and staples were the only things that worked while stocks and bonds bled. A hated, cheap, dividend-paying crop-protection name is how you position for it early.

tweets.text:
Japan just fired the biggest currency intervention in its history, and the US joined in for the first time in 30 years.

Thursday's yen buying hit roughly 8.45 trillion yen, about $52.8 billion in a single day. Then the New York Fed sold euros to buy yen for the US Treasury. The last time Washington and Tokyo intervened together was the 1990s.

The yen still sits near 157, a stone's throw from its weakest level since 1986.

Here is why the US cares. A yen in freefall forces Japan, the largest foreign holder of US Treasuries, to sell those bonds to fund the defense. It also threatens to unwind the carry trade, and hedge funds are sitting on $9.5 billion of short-yen bets. When the two biggest checkbooks on earth fire together and the currency barely moves, the next leg is a disorderly unwind that pushes up US yields and hits US stocks.
